screens.title: The Frontend dApp Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Before we dive into coding, let's visualize the fundamental architecture of a frontend dApp interacting with a Substrate chain. At its core, a decentralized application, or dApp, is simply a web application that uses a blockchain as its backend instead of a traditional centralized server. Your React, Vue, or vanilla JavaScript frontend serves as the user interface, providing buttons, input fields, and displays. This frontend doesn't directly talk to the blockchain. Instead, it communicates through a specialized library: the Polkadot-JS A P I. This A P I acts as a crucial intermediary, abstracting away the complexities of blockchain communication, allowing your dApp to send transactions, query chain state, and subscribe to real-time updates. The A P I then connects to your Substrate chain, typically via a WebSocket connection to a node. This layered approach ensures that your dApp remains user-friendly while securely and efficiently interacting with the decentralized ledger. It's a powerful model that combines the best of web development with the trust and transparency of blockchain technology. Understanding this flow is essential for building robust and secure dApps. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 5›Chapter 5.5›The Frontend dApp Architecture
Web3 Frontend Fundamentals

The Frontend dApp Architecture

Understanding how your web application interacts with a Substrate chain.

Key Components of a dApp

  • 1.
    User Interface (UI): Your web application (e.g., React) provides the visual and interactive elements for the user.
  • 2.
    Polkadot-JS API: A JavaScript library that facilitates communication between your frontend and the Substrate chain.
  • 3.
    Substrate Chain: The blockchain backend, hosting your custom logic (pallets) and state.
  • 4.
    Browser Extension: (e.g., Polkadot-JS Extension) Securely manages user accounts and signs transactions.
Key Takeaway

Frontend dApps leverage the Polkadot-JS API and browser extensions to provide a secure and user-friendly interface for interacting with a Substrate blockchain backend.

screens.title: The Polkadot-JS Browser Extension
screens.narratorSegment: The Polkadot-JS Browser Extension is a cornerstone of secure dApp interaction within the Polkadot and Substrate ecosystem. It acts as a secure key manager, fundamentally changing how your dApp handles user accounts and private keys. Crucially, this extension prevents your dApp from ever directly accessing a user's private keys. Instead, when your dApp needs to send a transaction, it requests the extension to sign that transaction on the user's behalf. This is a critical security measure, as it isolates sensitive cryptographic material from your dApp's code, significantly reducing the risk of private key exposure. For users, this means they must have the Polkadot-JS Extension installed in their browser, whether it's Chrome or Firefox, and they need to have their accounts, like Alice's development account, imported into it. The extension then provides a user-friendly interface for approving or rejecting transaction requests, giving users full control over their on-chain actions. This model ensures that while your dApp provides the interface and logic, the user always retains ultimate control and security over their digital assets. It's a vital component for building trustworthy and secure decentralized applications.

The Polkadot-JS Browser Extension

Understanding its role as a secure key manager for dApp interactions.

Extension's Core Functions

  • •
    Transaction Signing: Signs transactions on behalf of the dApp, requiring user approval.

screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's dive into the code and start building our React dApp. We'll begin by modifying the src slash App. jsx file, which is the main component of our React application. Inside this file, we'll use React's use State hook to manage various pieces of our application's state, such as the A P I instance, the current block number, and account balances. The use Effect hook will be crucial for handling side effects, like connecting to our Substrate node and setting up subscriptions. Our first use Effect block will be responsible for establishing the connection to our local Substrate node. We'll create a Ws Provider instance, pointing to our node's WebSocket endpoint, typically ws. slash slash 127.0.0.1. 9944. Then, we'll use Api Promise. create to initialize the Polkadot-JS A P I. Once the A P I is successfully connected, we'll store the A P I instance in our component's state using set Api. It's good practice to include a cleanup function within use Effect to disconnect the A P I when the component unmounts, preventing potential memory leaks. This initial setup is the gateway for your dApp to start interacting with the blockchain, laying the foundation for all subsequent data fetching and transaction sending.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.5›API Connection
Connecting to the Chain

Initial `App.jsx` Structure and API Connection

Setting up React state and establishing a connection to your local Substrate node.

Key Steps for API Connection

  • •
    Import Hooks: Bring in `useState` and `useEffect` from React.
  • •
    Initialize State: Declare state variables for `api`, `currentBlock`, `aliceBalance`, etc.
  • •
    Create Provider: Instantiate `WsProvider` with your node's WebSocket URL.
  • •
    Connect API: Use `ApiPromise.create` to establish the connection.
  • •
    Cleanup: Disconnect the API when the component unmounts to prevent leaks.
Key Takeaway

The `useEffect` hook is ideal for managing the lifecycle of your API connection, ensuring it's established on mount and cleaned up on unmount.

jsx
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { ApiPromise, WsProvider } from '@polkadot/api';

function App() {
  const [api, setApi] = useState(null);
  const [currentBlock, setCurrentBlock] = useState(0);
  const [aliceBalance, setAliceBalance] = useState('0');
  // ... other state variables

  useEffect(() => {
    const connectToSubstrate = async () => {
      const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944');
      const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider });
      setApi(api);
      console.log('Connected to Substrate node.');
    };

    connectToSubstrate();

    return () => {
      api && api.disconnect();
    };
  }, []); // Run once on component mount

  if (!api) {
    return <div>Connecting to Substrate...</div>;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>My Substrate DApp</h1>
      <p>Current Block: {currentBlock}</p>
      <p>Alice's Balance: {aliceBalance}</p>
    </div>
  );
}
API Connection

screens.title: Enabling the Polkadot-JS Extension and Loading Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: With our A P I connected, the next critical step is to integrate with the Polkadot-JS Browser Extension to access user accounts securely. This is where the @polkadot slash extension-dapp library comes into play. Inside our use Effect hook, after the A P I connection is established, we'll call web3Enable, passing the name of our dApp, for example, 'my-substrate-dapp'. This function initializes the connection to the browser extension and, importantly, prompts the user for permission to access their accounts. If the user hasn't installed the extension or denies permission, we should provide clear feedback, perhaps an alert, guiding them on what to do next. Once permission is granted, we can use web3Accounts to retrieve a list of all accounts managed by the extension that the user has authorized for our dApp. We'll store these accounts in our component's state and, for simplicity, select the first available account as the default. This process ensures that your dApp can interact with user accounts without ever needing to handle sensitive private keys directly, upholding the highest security standards for decentralized applications. It's a fundamental pattern for any dApp in the Polkadot ecosystem.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.5›User Accounts
Integrating User Accounts

Enabling the Polkadot-JS Extension and Loading Accounts

Accessing user accounts securely through the browser extension.

Extension Integration Flow

  1. Enable Extension: Call `web3Enable('your-dapp-name')` to prompt user for permission.
  2. Handle No Extension: Provide feedback if the extension is not found.
  3. Retrieve Accounts: Use `web3Accounts()` to get authorized accounts.
  4. Set Default Account: Select an initial account for interaction.

Common Mistake: Forgetting to call `web3Enable` will prevent your dApp from accessing any accounts from the extension.

Key Takeaway

The Polkadot-JS Extension is the secure gateway to user accounts; `web3Enable` and `web3Accounts` are the primary functions for integration.

jsx
// src/App.jsx
import { web3Accounts, web3Enable } from '@polkadot/extension-dapp';

// ... inside useEffect for API connection ...
    const connectToSubstrate = async () => {
      // ... API connection code ...

      // Enable the Polkadot-JS Extension
      const extensions = await web3Enable('my-substrate-dapp');
      if (extensions.length === 0) {
        alert('No Polkadot-JS Extension found. Please install it to interact with accounts.');
        return;
      }

      // Get all accounts from the extension
      const allAccounts = await web3Accounts();
      setAccounts(allAccounts);
      if (allAccounts.length > 0) {
        setSelectedAccount(allAccounts[0]); // Select the first account by default
      }
    };
// ...
Extension Integration

screens.title: Subscribing to Block Headers and Account Balances
screens.narratorSegment: A truly interactive dApp needs to display real-time information from the blockchain. This is achieved through subscriptions, where your dApp listens for updates from the Substrate node. We'll set up another use Effect hook, which will run whenever our A P I instance or the selected account changes. Inside this hook, we'll establish two key subscriptions. First, we'll subscribe to new block headers using api. rpc. chain. subscribe New Heads. This will provide us with a continuous stream of new block information, allowing us to update the current block number displayed in our UI. Second, and equally important, we'll subscribe to the selected account's balance using api. query. system. account open parenthesis selected Account. address close parenthesis. This subscription will automatically push updates to our dApp whenever the account's balance changes, ensuring the UI always reflects the latest state. It's crucial to manage these subscriptions properly. Each subscription returns an unsub function. We must call these unsub functions in the use Effect cleanup block to prevent memory leaks when the component unmounts or when the dependencies of the use Effect hook change. This pattern ensures efficient and dynamic display of blockchain data, making your dApp responsive and informative.

Second, and equally important, we'll subscribe to the selected account's balance using api. query. system. account open parenthesis selected Account. address close parenthesis. This subscription will automatically push updates to our dApp whenever the account's balance changes, ensuring the UI always reflects the latest state. It's crucial to manage these subscriptions properly. Each subscription returns an unsub function. content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.5›Chain Subscriptions
Real-time Chain State

Subscribing to Block Headers and Account Balances

Displaying dynamic blockchain data in your dApp's user interface.

Subscription Types

  • •
    Block Headers: `api.rpc.chain.subscribeNewHeads` provides continuous updates on new blocks.
  • •
    Account Balance: `api.query.system.account` tracks changes in a specific account's balance.

Common Mistake: Forgetting to unsubscribe (`unsubBlock()`, `unsubBalance()`) can lead to memory leaks and unexpected behavior in single-page applications.

Key Takeaway

Subscriptions are essential for real-time dApp updates, but always ensure proper cleanup with `unsub` functions to maintain application performance.

jsx
// src/App.jsx
// ... inside App function ...
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!api || !selectedAccount) return;

    let unsubBlock = null;
    let unsubBalance = null;

    const subscribeData = async () => {
      // Subscribe to new block headers
      unsubBlock = await api.rpc.chain.subscribeNewHeads((header) => {
        setCurrentBlock(header.number.toNumber());
      });

      // Subscribe to selected account's balance
      unsubBalance = await api.query.system.account(selectedAccount.address, ({ data: balance }) => {
        setAliceBalance(balance.free.toHuman());
      });
    };

    subscribeData();

    // Cleanup subscriptions
    return () => {
      unsubBlock && unsubBlock();
      unsubBalance && unsubBalance();
    };
  }, [api, selectedAccount]); // Re-subscribe if API or selected account changes
// ...
Real-time Data

Handling Account Selection in the UI

Allowing users to choose their active account for dApp interactions.

Account Selection Logic

  • •

    Dynamic Updates: Changing the selected account triggers re-subscription to its balance.

UX Tip: Always show a clear indicator of the currently selected account and its associated balance to avoid user confusion.

Key Takeaway

Providing a clear account selection mechanism is crucial for dApp usability, ensuring users can easily manage their on-chain identity and assets.

jsx
// src/App.jsx
// ... inside App function ...
  const handleAccountChange = (event) => {
    const selected = accounts.find(acc => acc.address === event.target.value);
    setSelectedAccount(selected);
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Account Info</h2>
      {accounts.length > 0 ? (
        <div>
          <label htmlFor="account-select">Select Account:</label>
          <select id="account-select" onChange={handleAccountChange} value={selectedAccount?.address || ''}>
            {accounts.map(account => (
              <option key={account.address} value={account.address}>
                {account.meta.name} ({account.address.slice(0, 6)}...{account.address.slice(-4)})
              </option>
            ))}
          </select>
          {selectedAccount && (
            <p>Selected Account Balance: {aliceBalance} {api.registry.chainTokens[0]}</p>
          )}
        </div>
      ) : (
        <p>No accounts found. Please ensure Polkadot-JS Extension is installed and has accounts.</p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Module 5›Chapter 5.5›Transaction Logic
Sending Extrinsics

Implementing the Transaction Logic

Constructing and preparing a balance transfer extrinsic for signing.

Key Steps in `handleTransfer`

  • •
    Input Validation: Check for filled fields and selected account.
  • •
    Get Injector: Use `web3FromSource(selectedAccount.meta.source)` to get the signing mechanism.
  • •
    Format Amount: Convert human-readable amount to chain's smallest unit (plancks) using `api.registry.chainDecimals`.
  • •
    Create Extrinsic: Construct the transaction, e.g., `api.tx.balances.transfer(recipient, amount)`.
Key Takeaway

Correctly obtaining the `injector` and formatting transaction amounts are crucial steps before signing and sending any extrinsic via the browser extension.

jsx
// src/App.jsx
import { web3FromSource } from '@polkadot/extension-dapp';

// ... inside App function ...
  const handleTransfer = async () => {
    if (!api || !selectedAccount || !transferAmount || !recipientAddress) {
      alert('Please fill all transfer fields and select an account.');
      return;
    }

    setStatus('Sending transaction...');
    try {
      const injector = await web3FromSource(selectedAccount.meta.source);
      const transferValue = api.registry.createType(
        'Balance',
        parseFloat(transferAmount) * Math.pow(10, api.registry.chainDecimals)
      );
      const tx = api.tx.balances.transfer(recipientAddress, transferValue);

      // ... signAndSend will go here ...

    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Error sending transfer:', error);
      setStatus(`Error: ${error.message}`);
    }
  };
// ...
Transfer Logic

screens.title: Signing and Sending Transactions with the Extension
screens.narratorSegment: Once the transaction extrinsic is constructed, the next step is to sign and send it. This is where the Polkadot-JS Extension plays its crucial role in user security. We'll call tx. sign And Send, passing the selected Account. address and an options object containing the signer from our injector. When this line of code executes, the Polkadot-JS Extension will automatically pop up a confirmation window in the user's browser. This window allows the user to review all the details of the transaction, such as the recipient, amount, and associated fees, before explicitly approving or rejecting it. This user approval step is a fundamental security feature, ensuring that no transaction is sent without the user's explicit consent. The sign And Send method also takes a callback function that provides real-time status updates on the transaction's journey. You'll receive updates as the transaction is is In Block, meaning it has been included in a block, and finally when it is Finalized, indicating it's irreversibly committed to the chain. It's also vital to handle dispatch Error to inform the user if the transaction failed and why. By monitoring these statuses and providing clear feedback, your dApp offers a transparent and trustworthy transaction experience. This complete flow, from construction to signing and status updates, forms the backbone of interactive dApp functionality.

Module 5›Chapter 5.5›Signing & Status
Transaction Lifecycle

Signing and Sending Transactions with the Extension

Guiding users through transaction approval and monitoring status updates.

Transaction Flow Steps

  • •
    `signAndSend`: Initiates the signing process using the extension's `signer`.
  • •
    User Approval: Extension prompts user to review and approve the transaction.
  • •
    Status Updates: Callback provides real-time status (`isInBlock`, `isFinalized`).
  • •
    Error Handling: Check `dispatchError` for transaction failures and provide feedback.
Key Takeaway

The `signAndSend` method, combined with the extension's `signer`, enables secure user-approved transactions and provides crucial status feedback for a robust dApp experience.

jsx
// src/App.jsx
// ... inside handleTransfer function ...
      await tx.signAndSend(selectedAccount.address, { signer: injector.signer }, ({ status, events, dispatchError }) => {
        if (status.isInBlock) {
          setStatus(`Transaction in block: ${status.asInBlock.toHex()}`);
        }
        if (status.isFinalized) {
          if (dispatchError) {
            if (dispatchError.isModule) {
              const decoded = api.registry.findError(dispatchError.asModule);
              setStatus(`Transfer failed: ${decoded.section}.${decoded.name}`);
            } else {
              setStatus(`Transfer failed: ${dispatchError.toString()}`);
            }
          } else {
            setStatus(`Transfer finalized! Block: ${status.asFinalized.toHex()}`);
            events.forEach(({ event }) => {
              if (event.section === 'balances' && event.method === 'Transfer') {
                const [from, to, amount] = event.data;
                console.log(`Transfer event: ${from.toHuman()} -> ${to.toHuman()} (${amount.toHuman()})`);
              }
            });
          }
        }
      });
// ...
Signing & Status

screens.title: Common Mistakes in Frontend dApp Development
screens.narratorSegment: As you build frontend dApps, you'll inevitably encounter common challenges. Being aware of these pitfalls can save you significant debugging time. One frequent mistake is forgetting to call web3Enable at the start of your application. Without this, your dApp won't be able to access any accounts from the Polkadot-JS Extension, leading to a non-functional account selection. Another critical oversight is not handling unsub functions for A P I listeners. Subscriptions to block headers or account balances, if not properly unsubscribed when a component unmounts or re-renders, can cause memory leaks and degrade your application's performance over time. Incorrect amount calculation is also a common issue; always remember to multiply user-entered amounts by 10 to the power of chain Decimals before sending them to the chain, as the blockchain operates on the smallest unit. From a security perspective, never, under any circumstances, ask users for their seed phrases or private keys directly in your dApp. Always rely on the browser extension for secure key management. Finally, prioritize user experience by providing clear status updates for transactions and guiding users through extension permissions. A well-designed UI with informative feedback builds trust and makes your dApp a pleasure to use. By avoiding these common mistakes, you'll build more reliable, secure, and user-friendly decentralized applications.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to a pivotal chapter where we bridge the gap between your Substrate blockchain and a user-friendly web interface. Up until now, you've mastered programmatic interaction with the Polkadot-JS A P I in Node. js, but the true power of Web3 emerges when users can engage with your decentralized logic through a familiar web browser. This lesson will guide you through the essential steps of integrating the Polkadot-JS A P I into a simple frontend project, allowing you to display real-time chain data and enable basic transaction sending. We'll focus on a React application, a popular choice for dApp development, but the core principles you learn here are universally applicable across other JavaScript frameworks like Vue or Svelte. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a foundational understanding of how to create an interactive gateway to your Substrate chain, making your decentralized application accessible and usable for everyone.

In this chapter, we'll equip you with the fundamental skills to build compelling frontend applications that interact seamlessly with your Substrate chain. Our first objective is to help you understand the basic architecture of a frontend dApp, clarifying how it connects and communicates with a Substrate chain. This foundational knowledge is crucial for designing robust and efficient decentralized applications. Next, you'll learn how to set up a modern JavaScript frontend project, specifically using React with Vite, a popular and efficient toolchain for dApp development. To begin building our frontend dApp, we'll use React, a popular and efficient JavaScript library for user interfaces, combined with Vite, a next-generation frontend tooling that offers incredibly fast development. This extension is the standard and most secure way for users to manage their accounts and sign transactions in a browser environment, keeping their private keys safe. These commands lay the groundwork for your dApp, providing all the tools you need to connect and interact with your Substrate chain.

The Polkadot-JS Browser Extension is a cornerstone of secure dApp interaction within the Polkadot and Substrate ecosystem. It acts as a secure key manager, fundamentally changing how your dApp handles user accounts and private keys. Crucially, this extension prevents your dApp from ever directly accessing a user's private keys. Instead, when your dApp needs to send a transaction, it requests the extension to sign that transaction on the user's behalf. This is a critical security measure, as it isolates sensitive cryptographic material from your dApp's code, significantly reducing the risk of private key exposure. For users, this means they must have the Polkadot-JS Extension installed in their browser, whether it's Chrome or Firefox, and they need to have their accounts, like Alice's development account, imported into it. The extension then provides a user-friendly interface for approving or rejecting transaction requests, giving users full control over their on-chain actions. This model ensures that while your dApp provides the interface and logic, the user always retains ultimate control and security over their digital assets. It's a vital component for building trustworthy and secure decentralized applications.

Now, let's dive into the code and start building our React dApp. We'll begin by modifying the src slash App. jsx file, which is the main component of our React application. Inside this file, we'll use React's use State hook to manage various pieces of our application's state, such as the A P I instance, the current block number, and account balances. The use Effect hook will be crucial for handling side effects, like connecting to our Substrate node and setting up subscriptions. Our first use Effect block will be responsible for establishing the connection to our local Substrate node. We'll create a Ws Provider instance, pointing to our node's WebSocket endpoint, typically ws. slash slash 127.0.0.1. 9944. Then, we'll use Api Promise. create to initialize the Polkadot-JS A P I. Once the A P I is successfully connected, we'll store the A P I instance in our component's state using set Api. It's good practice to include a cleanup function within use Effect to disconnect the A P I when the component unmounts, preventing potential memory leaks. This initial setup is the gateway for your dApp to start interacting with the blockchain, laying the foundation for all subsequent data fetching and transaction sending.

With our A P I connected, the next critical step is to integrate with the Polkadot-JS Browser Extension to access user accounts securely. This is where the @polkadot slash extension-dapp library comes into play. Inside our use Effect hook, after the A P I connection is established, we'll call web3Enable, passing the name of our dApp, for example, 'my-substrate-dapp'. This function initializes the connection to the browser extension and, importantly, prompts the user for permission to access their accounts. If the user hasn't installed the extension or denies permission, we should provide clear feedback, perhaps an alert, guiding them on what to do next. Once permission is granted, we can use web3Accounts to retrieve a list of all accounts managed by the extension that the user has authorized for our dApp. We'll store these accounts in our component's state and, for simplicity, select the first available account as the default. This process ensures that your dApp can interact with user accounts without ever needing to handle sensitive private keys directly, upholding the highest security standards for decentralized applications. It's a fundamental pattern for any dApp in the Polkadot ecosystem.

A truly interactive dApp needs to display real-time information from the blockchain. This is achieved through subscriptions, where your dApp listens for updates from the Substrate node. We'll set up another use Effect hook, which will run whenever our A P I instance or the selected account changes. Inside this hook, we'll establish two key subscriptions. First, we'll subscribe to new block headers using api. rpc. chain. subscribe New Heads. This will provide us with a continuous stream of new block information, allowing us to update the current block number displayed in our UI. Second, and equally important, we'll subscribe to the selected account's balance using api. query. system. account open parenthesis selected Account. address close parenthesis. This subscription will automatically push updates to our dApp whenever the account's balance changes, ensuring the UI always reflects the latest state. It's crucial to manage these subscriptions properly. Each subscription returns an unsub function. We must call these unsub functions in the use Effect cleanup block to prevent memory leaks when the component unmounts or when the dependencies of the use Effect hook change. This pattern ensures efficient and dynamic display of blockchain data, making your dApp responsive and informative.

For a dApp to be truly user-friendly, it must allow users to select which of their authorized accounts they want to use for interactions. This is typically achieved through a dropdown menu or a similar UI element. In our React application, we'll implement a select element that displays all the accounts retrieved from the Polkadot-JS Extension. Each option in the dropdown will represent an account, showing its name and a truncated address for easy identification. We'll manage the currently selected account using our selected Account state variable. When a user changes their selection in the dropdown, our handle Account Change function will be triggered. This function will find the corresponding account object from our accounts array based on the selected address and then update the selected Account state. This change will, in turn, trigger our balance subscription use Effect hook to re-subscribe to the newly selected account's balance, ensuring the UI always reflects the correct information. This seamless account switching is a fundamental aspect of good dApp user experience, providing flexibility and control to the user. It's a small but crucial detail that significantly enhances the usability of your decentralized application.

Now that we can connect to the chain and manage accounts, let's enable users to send transactions. We'll implement a handle Transfer function that will be triggered when a user clicks a 'Send Transfer' button. This function first performs basic validation to ensure all necessary fields, like recipient address and amount, are filled and an account is selected. The core of sending a transaction securely through the browser extension involves obtaining an injector object. We get this using web3From Source, passing the source of our selected Account's metadata, which tells us which extension manages that account. The injector contains the signer object, which is crucial for the next step. Before creating the transaction, we must correctly format the transfer amount. User-entered amounts are typically in human-readable units, but the blockchain expects values in its smallest unit, often called 'plancks'. So, we'll convert the transfer Amount by multiplying it by 10 raised to the power of the chain's decimal places, using api. registry. chain Decimals. Finally, we construct the actual transaction using api. tx. balances. transfer, providing the recipient's address and the correctly formatted amount. This prepared transaction is then ready to be signed and sent, which we'll cover next.

Once the transaction extrinsic is constructed, the next step is to sign and send it. This is where the Polkadot-JS Extension plays its crucial role in user security. We'll call tx. sign And Send, passing the selected Account. address and an options object containing the signer from our injector. When this line of code executes, the Polkadot-JS Extension will automatically pop up a confirmation window in the user's browser. This window allows the user to review all the details of the transaction, such as the recipient, amount, and associated fees, before explicitly approving or rejecting it. This user approval step is a fundamental security feature, ensuring that no transaction is sent without the user's explicit consent. The sign And Send method also takes a callback function that provides real-time status updates on the transaction's journey. You'll receive updates as the transaction is is In Block, meaning it has been included in a block, and finally when it is Finalized, indicating it's irreversibly committed to the chain. It's also vital to handle dispatch Error to inform the user if the transaction failed and why. By monitoring these statuses and providing clear feedback, your dApp offers a transparent and trustworthy transaction experience. As you build frontend dApps, you'll inevitably encounter common challenges. Being aware of these pitfalls can save you significant debugging time. One frequent mistake is forgetting to call web3Enable at the start of your application. Without this, your dApp won't be able to access any accounts from the Polkadot-JS Extension, leading to a non-functional account selection. Another critical oversight is not handling unsub functions for A P I listeners. Subscriptions to block headers or account balances, if not properly unsubscribed when a component unmounts or re-renders, can cause memory leaks and degrade your application's performance over time. Incorrect amount calculation is also a common issue; always remember to multiply user-entered amounts by 10 to the power of chain Decimals before sending them to the chain, as the blockchain operates on the smallest unit. From a security perspective, never, under any circumstances, ask users for their seed phrases or private keys directly in your dApp. Always rely on the browser extension for secure key management. Finally, prioritize user experience by providing clear status updates for transactions and guiding users through extension permissions. A well-designed UI with informative feedback builds trust and makes your dApp a pleasure to use. By avoiding these common mistakes, you'll build more reliable, secure, and user-friendly decentralized applications.
